text: A 45-year-old patient undergoes complete ileal and partial jejunal resection due to Crohn's disease. Which of the following deficiencies is he most likely to develop in the long term?
expl: Explanation: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is absorbed primarily in the terminal ileum after binding to intrinsic factor (IF) secreted by gastric parietal cells. Complete ileal resection → impaired B12 absorption → megaloblastic anemia and neurological symptoms (paresthesia, memory impairment). Jejunal resection affects absorption of carbohydrates, proteins, fats, and some vitamins, but does not significantly impact B12 absorption , which occurs mainly in the ileum. Therefore, Vitamin B12 deficiency is the most immediate and predictable outcome. Ileum resection: B12, bile salts → fat malabsorption, steatorrhea Jejunum resection: Carbs, proteins, water-soluble vitamins → malnutrition, diarrhea Explanation of Other Options: Folic acid deficiency (Option A): Absorbed in proximal small intestine (duodenum, jejunum). Only a minor portion of the jejunum is resected → folate absorption may be partially affected, but B12 deficiency is more likely. Gastric ulcer (Option C) : Not directly caused by ileal or jejunal resection. Gastric acid secretion or IF may be affected indirectly by B12 deficiency but does not cause ulceration. Constipation (Option D) : May occur due to decreased bowel length or malabsorption, but not the most likely or direct consequence compared to B12 deficiency. Key Takeaway Points: Site of Vitamin Absorption in Small Intestine Clinical Correlation: Vitamin B12 deficiency signs: Megaloblastic anemia (macrocytosis) Neurological: peripheral neuropathy, subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord Management: Lifelong B12 supplementation (oral if some ileum remains; otherwise parenteral).

text: An 18-year-old was brought to the emergency department by her friends as she had turned blue. She was well otherwise. On examination she has central cyanosis; all other parameters are normal. What is the most likely cause?
expl: The question deals with cyanosis in an otherwise well patient. Cyanosis is seen in hypoxia. But the patient with hypoxia will be dyspnoeic. Here the patient is otherwise normal. Rare cause of cyanosis is due to abnormal hemoglobins like methemoglobin or Sulfhemoglobin. The causes of methemoglobinemia includes: Nitrates, nitric oxide or nitrobenzene Aniline dyes Propanil(a herbicide) Dapsone Pyridium So the accurate among the options are drinking water contaminated with nitrates. Lead poisoning will not lead to cyanosis but bluish lines in the gums. Carbon monoxide poisoning will cause cherry red discolouration. Anorexia nervosa is a disease of distorted perception of body image, where the patient restricts food intake and will be malnourished. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch:459 Pg 3593

text: A patient presents to the OPD with a history of diarrhoea after consuming a salad. What is the most likely organism responsible for this illness?
expl: Explanation: Staphylococcus aureus causes food poisoning due to ingestion of preformed enterotoxin , often found in improperly stored salads, dairy products, and bakery foods . The illness is characterised by a rapid onset (1-6 hours) of vomiting, abdominal cramps, and sometimes diarrhoea . Because the toxin is preformed, antibiotics are not useful; management is supportive. Explanation of other options: Bacillus cereus (Option B): Classically linked to reheated rice ("fried rice syndrome"), not fresh salads. text: A patient is diagnosed with an ileal tumor, with elevated urinary 5-HIAA levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?

text: All of the following tests are done for screening in patients with Turner's syndrome, except?
expl: Explanation: Turner syndrome is a genetic condition caused by the complete or partial absence of one X chromosome. Individuals with Turner syndrome require lifelong, multidisciplinary care to monitor and manage associated health complications. The ANA test is not typically performed as part of Turner mosaic screening. ANA testing is primarily used to help diagnose autoimmune conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or other connective tissue diseases. Explanation of other options: Audiometry (Option B): This test is a standard and recurring part of care. Individuals with Turner syndrome have a very high prevalence of hearing issues, including conductive hearing loss from frequent otitis media and sensorineural hearing loss . Therefore, serial audiology evaluations are mandated throughout their lifespan. Echocardiography (Option C): This is a critical and mandatory screening tool, not an exception. Cardiovascular anomalies are among the most serious complications of Turner syndrome. An echocardiogram is required to diagnose and monitor conditions like bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation of the aorta, and aortic dilation/ dissection , which are significant causes of morbidity and require ongoing surveillance. Fasting Blood Glucose (Option D): Screening for metabolic disorders is a standard practice. Due to an increased risk of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes , regular assessment of fasting glucose (and often hemoglobin A1c) is a core part of the annual health evaluation for adolescents and adults with Turner syndrome. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK554621/

text: A patient with hemolytic anemia presents with dactylitis and chest pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Symptoms of dactylitis and chest pain in a patient with hemolytic anemia are characteristic of a sickling crisis , seen in sickle cell disease due to vaso-occlusion by sickled RBCs. Sickle cell disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a point mutation on chromosome 11 , where glutamic acid is replaced by valine at position 6 of the β-globin chain . This mutation produces abnormal hemoglobin (HbS) , which polymerizes under low oxygen tension , causing red blood cells to become sickle-shaped, rigid, and fragile . These deformed cells lead to vaso-occlusion , tissue ischemia , and hemolysis , resulting in the characteristic acute painful crises . The term "sickle cell crisis" includes several acute manifestations such as vaso-occlusive crisis , aplastic crisis , splenic sequestration crisis , hyperhaemolysis crisis , hepatic crisis , dactylitis , and acute chest syndrome . Types of Sickle Cell Crises Explanation of other options: Microangiopathic anaemia (Option A): Occurs due to mechanical destruction of RBCs as they pass through damaged small vessels, as in DIC, HSP. Schistocytes (fragmented RBCs) are seen on peripheral smear. It does not cause dactylitis or chest pain. Intravascular haemolysis (Option C): Refers to the destruction of RBCs within blood vessels, releasing free haemoglobin, causing haemoglobinemia, haemoglobinuria, and jaundice. It is a mechanism of anaemia, not a specific disease causing vaso-occlusion or dactylitis. text: Which of the following is true regarding laboratory findings of Zieve's Syndrome?
expl: A unique form of hemolytic anemia (with spur cells and acanthocytes) called Zieve's syndrome can occur in patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis. Platelet counts are often reduced early in the disease, reflective of portal hypertension with hypersplenism. Serum total bilirubin can be normal or elevated with advanced disease. Prothrombin times are often prolonged and usually do not respond to administration of parenteral vitamin K. text: A 45 year old man presents with acute, profuse, watery diarrhea some days after returning from a holiday. Which one of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

text: Drug of choice for treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is
expl: Nitrofurantoin, ampicillin, and cephalosporins are considered relatively safe in early pregnancy. Generally, pregnant women with ASB are treated for 4-7 days in the absence of evidence to support single-dose therapy. text: What is the drug of choice for Legionnaire's disease?
expl: Explanation: Azithromycin is the preferred agent for treating Legionnaire's disease due to its superior efficacy, better tolerability, and lower potential for drug interactions compared to erythromycin. Legionella Features: Thin, Gram-negative, non-capsulated bacilli. Poor Gram staining; best visualized by Direct Fluorescent Antibody (DFA) staining. Requires Buffered Charcoal Yeast Extract (BCYE) agar for growth. Mode of Infection: Microaspiration and aerosol inhalation; no human-to-human transmission. Epidemiology: Associated with air conditioners, showers, coolers; commonly seen in smokers, immunocompromised, and elderly patients. Treatment: First-line: Macrolides [Azithromycin preferred over Erythromycin], ciprofloxacin, tetracyclines. Severe cases: Rifampicin may be added. Ineffective: Beta-lactams and aminoglycosides. Explanation of other options: Vancomycin (Option A): Active against Gram-positive bacteria like Staphylococcus and Enterococcus; ineffective for Legionella. Streptomycin (Option C): Aminoglycoside used in TB and plague; lacks efficacy against Legionella. Erythromycin (Option D): Previously first-line, now replaced by Azithromycin due to better tolerability. References: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK7619/

text: What is the treatment of choice for restless leg syndrome?
expl: Most RLS sufferers have mild symptoms that do not require specific treatment. General measures to improve sleep hygiene and quality should be attempted first. If symptoms remain intrusive, low doses of dopamine agonists, e.g., pramipexole (0.25-0.5 mg), ropinirole (1-2 mg), or patch rotigotine (2-3 mg), taken 1-2 h before bedtime are generally effective. Levodopa may also be effective but is more likely to be associated with augmentation (spread and worsening of restlessness and its appearance earlier in the day) or rebound (reappearance sometimes with worsening of symptoms at a time related to the drug's short half-life). Augmentation can also be seen with dopamine agonists, particularly if higher doses are employed. Other drugs that can be effective include anticonvulsants, analgesics, and opiates. Management of secondary RLS should be directed to correcting the underlying disorder; for example, iron replacement for anemia. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 436, Pg: 3402

text: Treatment of choice in young patients with AML is

options.A: Inj Cytarabine (100-200mg/m2) + Inj Daunorubicin (60-90 mg/m2) [7+3 regimen]
options.B: Inj Cytarabine (100-200mg/m2) + Inj Daunorubicin (60-90 mg/m2) [3+7 regimen]

ansText: Inj Cytarabine (100-200mg/m2) + Inj Daunorubicin (60-90 mg/m2) [7+3 regimen]
expl: The treatment for acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is divided into two phases - induction and postremission management (consolidation). The initial goal is to induce complete remission. The regimen most commonly used in younger patients is - Cytarabine (S-phase–specific antimetabolite) used at standard dose (100-200 mg/m 2 ) is administered as a continuous intravenous infusion for 7 days . With cytarabine, anthracycline therapy (DNA intercalator) generally consists of daunorubicin (60-90 mg/m 2 ) or idarubicin (12 mg/m 2 ) intravenously on days 1, 2, and 3 ( the 7 and 3 regimen ). With the 7 and 3 regimen, it is now clearly established that 45 mg/m 2 dosing of daunorubicin results in inferior outcomes. Older patients , especially those >65 years or with adverse risk disease, or those who are unfit for intensive anthracycline + cytarabine regimens, may be considered for investigational therapy alone or in combination with lower intensity chemotherapy (azacitidine, decitabine, cytarabine), or lower intensity chemotherapy in combination with venetoclax. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 104, Pg: 813

text: What is the recommended immediate medical treatment for a patient with a severe history of a road traffic accident who exhibits signs of elevated intracranial pressure upon examination?

options.B: Initiate anticoagulant therapy to prevent blood clot formation

expl: Explanation: In a trauma patient with signs of elevated intracranial pressure (ICP), the immediate goal is to reduce brain edema and prevent herniation. Mannitol is a first-line hyperosmolar agent used for this purpose. Mechanism of Action Osmotic Effect: Mannitol creates an osmotic gradient that draws water out of the brain parenchyma (across an intact blood-brain barrier) into the vasculature, reducing cerebral edema and intracranial volume. Rheologic Effect: It temporarily expands plasma volume, reduces blood viscosity, and improves cerebral blood flow and oxygen delivery. Explanation of other options: Administer antibiotics (Option A): Antibiotics are crucial for preventing infection in open skull fractures or base of skull fractures with CSF leak, but they do not directly address acute raised ICP. Initiate anticoagulant therapy (Option B): Anticoagulants are contraindicated in the acute phase of traumatic brain injury due to the high risk of promoting or worsening intracranial hemorrhage. Perform immediate surgical intervention (Option C): Surgery (e.g., evacuation of a hematoma, decompressive craniectomy) may be the definitive treatment, but it requires prior imaging (CT scan) to identify the surgical lesion. Medical management with agents like mannitol is often initiated before or while preparing for surgery to stabilize the patient. Key Takeaways: Mannitol (or hypertonic saline) is a key medical therapy for rapidly lowering raised ICP in traumatic brain injury. Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10329884/

text: A 40-year-old patient presents with chronic diarrhea, fatigue, and exhibits the nail findings shown below (Koilonychia). Hemoglobin is 8 gm%. What is the most appropriate treatment?
expl: Explanation: The presentation of microcytic anemia (implied by low Hb) with Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails) is pathognomonic for chronic, severe Iron Deficiency Anemia . The chronic diarrhoea suggests a possible gastrointestinal source of blood loss or malabsorption. Rationale for Treatment Iron Supplementation: This is the definitive treatment to correct the deficiency and replenish stores. It addresses the root cause of the anemia and the associated nail changes. Investigate the Cause: The chronic diarrhea necessitates investigation for underlying GI pathology like celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, or a occult bleeding source. Explanation of other options: Folic acid & Vitamin B12 (Option A and D): These are used to treat macrocytic anaemia's, not microcytic anaemia. Koilonychia is not a feature of these deficiencies. Metronidazole(Option B): This is an antibiotic/antiparasitic agent. It would only be indicated if a specific infection (e.g., giardiasis) causing the diarrhoea and malabsorption were diagnosed, but it does not treat the iron deficiency itself. Key Takeaways: Koilonychia is a classic sign of severe, long-standing Iron Deficiency Anemia. The presence of anemia with GI symptoms like diarrhea should prompt a search for a GI cause of iron loss or malabsorption

text: A 30 year old male who was staying in Cuba for the past one year, now comes with history of chronic diarrhoea, weight loss and multiple nutritional deficiencies. He had tried stopping wheat and barley in his diet, but with no improvement in symptoms. A small bowel biopsy showed villous blunting with dense mononuclear infiltrate. The tissue transglutaminase antibody is negative. What will be the next best step?

options.A: Broad spectrum antibiotics with folate supplementation

ansText: Broad spectrum antibiotics with folate supplementation
expl: The history of malabsorption with a recent stay in Cuba points to the diagnosis of Tropical sprue. However, it could be a refractory celiac disease also, where the patient stops responding to gluten restriction, will have negative antibody screen and have active histopathological findings. In such cases an HLA DQ testing should be the next best step. But here since the history states that he is coming from a country in the tropics, a course of antibiotics and folate supplementation will be the next best cost effective step. Tropical sprue is considered to be post infectious complication. It is seen in countries like Southern India, Phillipines, Puerto- Rico, Pakistan and Cuba. It is characterized by severe malabsorption and two or more unrelated nutritional deficiencies including Vitamin B12 and Folic acid. text: A 70-year-old male presents with progressive dysphagia for solids, significant weight loss, and cachexia over the past few months. Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation for this patient?
expl: Explanation: The presentation of progressive dysphagia for solids with significant weight loss and cachexia in an elderly patient strongly suggests oesophageal carcinoma. UGIE also permits thorough examination of the larynx, trachea, and bronchi, which is crucial as this population has a higher risk of head and neck malignancies. Additionally, CT scanning of the chest and abdomen is typically performed to assess tumour spread to mediastinal and para-aortic lymph nodes. Barium meal follow through (Option D) : Primarily used to evaluate the small intestine and helps in evaluating suspected malabsorption, Crohn's disease etc.

text: A 27-year-old man is noted to have cyanosis of the lower limbs and clubbing of the toes but not the fingers. The blood pressure in the arm and lower limb is the same. Which of the following statements is true?

expl: Differential cyanosis (cyanosis only in lower extremities) is seen in a patient with patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) when there is reversal of shunt. Continuous machinery murmur is the classic murmur of PDA but when the shunt reverses (as in patients with a large PDA and/or pulmonary disease) the murmur becomes softer and shorter. text: Dystrophin absent and presence of small muscle fibrils cause?
expl: Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy are the Dystrophinopaties. DMD is characterized by absent dystrophin and Becker's muscular dystrophy is characterized by either decreased level or size of dystrophin. Total absence of dystrophin points to the diagnosis of DMD. Biopsy is not diagnostic in myopathies. So the microscopy will be almost the same for DMD and BMD. Muscle biopsy in young ages will show degeneration and regeneration of muscle fibres with preserved architecture. There is no active inflammation except for myophagocytosis. As the disease progresses, the muscle fibers are replaced by fatty infiltration. The remaining muscle fibers show varying size from atrophic to hypertrophic. Immunohistochemical staining shows absence of sarcolemmal staining in DMD and reduced staining in BMD. They are both XL recessive inheritance. Dystrophin provides stability to the muscle fibre by acting as a bridge between the cytoskeleton inside the muscle fibre and the basement membrane outside the cell. DMD results from deletions or frameshift mutations in the dystrophin gene, leading to total absence of the protein, whereas BMD results in the formation of truncated variant of dystrophin that leads to partially functional protein.

text: A 32 year old woman has a 3 month history of arthralgia joint pain and early morning stiffness. There is swelling of the distal interphalangeal joints of the ring fingers of the hand. expl: The presence of joint pains and early morning stiffness points towards an inflammatory arthritis. The patient in the given question is suffering from an asymmetric oligoarthritis, with involvement of DIP, which rules out RA. The sparing of large proximal joints and the age of the patient speaks against a Polymyalgia rheumatica. There are no other indicators to suggest a chronic gout, like tophi. An asymmetric oligoarthritis with onycholysis points to the diagnosis of Psoriatic Arthritis. text: For which of the following groups is pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine not routinely recommended?

options.A: Otherwise healthy adults aged 50 to 65 years
options.B: Adults aged 19 to 65 years who have immunocompromising conditions

ansText: Otherwise healthy adults aged 50 to 65 years
expl: Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine is not recommended for otherwise healthy adults aged 50 to 65 years. This vaccine is, however recommended for persons who have immunocompromising conditions or lung disease (such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or asthma) and for persons who are cigarette smokers and heavy consumers of alcohol. Post splenectomy or hyposplenism is another indication There are 2 types of pneumococcal vaccine pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) and a protein conjugate pneumococcal vaccine (PCV13) Routine use of PCV13 is recommended among adults aged 65 and older . Individuals 65 years of age or older who have never received a pneumococcal vaccine should first receive PCV13 followed by a dose of PPSV23 6-12 months later . text: A 35-year-old woman presents with fever, shortness of breath, and productive cough with expectoration. A CT chest scan was performed (shown below). What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The combination of fever, dyspnea, and expectoration , along with CT findings of consolidation accompanied by an air bronchogram , is highly suggestive of lobar pneumonia leading to pneumonic consolidation . Clinical manifestations of Lobar Pneumonia Common Symptoms: Fever Cough Mucopurulent sputum production Pleuritic chest pain (localized, sharp pain - especially in lobar disease) Constitutional Symptoms: Fatigue, headache, myalgia, arthralgia Severe Cases: Dyspnea Confusion, sepsis, multi-organ dysfunction Clinical Signs Respiratory signs: Tachypnea (↑ respiratory rate) Increased vocal fremitus Egophony (E-to-A changes) Dullness on percussion Crackles/rales and bronchial breath sounds (tubular type) Investigations & Findings Initial Evaluation: Based on history and clinical exam Chest Radiography: Most important initial test for pneumonia Detects pulmonary infiltrates (lobar, interstitial, unilateral, or bilateral) Cannot reliably separate bacterial vs. non-bacterial causes CT Scan: More sensitive than chest X-ray Dense opacification of an entire lobe with sparing of major airways May show ground-glass opacities and lobar/segmental pattern of involvement Image finding: Left upper lobe consolidation of heterogeneous density with multiple air bronchograms and a small pleural effusion Laboratory Tests: CBC: Leukocytosis (left shift) → infection marker; leukopenia → poor prognosis Inflammatory markers: ESR, acute phase reactants Sputum Analysis: Gram stain and culture critical in suspected lobar pneumonia Culture = most specific diagnostic test Influenza Testing: Recommended in winter due to co-infection risk Risk Stratification: CURB-65 / Pneumonia Severity Index → hospitalization decisions Other Diagnostic Measures: Blood cultures, urine antigen tests (before antibiotics) Thoracocentesis, bronchoscopy, pleural biopsy/culture (rare) Open lung biopsy = gold standard diagnostic test Explanation of Other Options Mediastinal Mass (Option B): Causes chest pain, cough, dyspnea, but not classical pneumonia features (fever, productive cough). Appears as a well-defined localized lesion with mass effect in mediastinum. Pleural Effusion (Option C): Appears on CT as fluid collection in pleural cavity. Leads to breathlessness, but not consolidation with air bronchograms. Typical finding = homogeneous pleural opacity. Diaphragmatic Hernia (Option D): On CT shows abdominal organs (stomach/bowel) in thoracic cavity . Not associated with fever, expectoration, or pulmonary consolidation. Key Takeaways Air bronchogram within consolidation is a hallmark of lobar pneumonia. Diagnosis requires clinical-radiological correlation. CT is more sensitive, but X-ray remains the first-line test . Always confirm etiology with sputum culture when possible. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK534295/ https://radiopaedia.org/articles/lobar-pneumonia

text: A physician is evaluating a patient for an occupational disease and finds that a coproporphyrin test has been performed. Which of the following conditions is most likely suspected?
expl: Explanation of answer: Lead poisoning disrupts heme biosynthesis, resulting in elevated urinary coproporphyrin , making it a key diagnostic clue. Lead poisoning, particularly from occupational exposure, interferes with heme synthesis by inhibiting several key enzymes such as δ-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase (ALAD) and ferrochelatase, leading to accumulation of heme precursors including coproporphyrin and δ-ALA (aminolevulinic acid) in the urine. Investigations in Lead Poisoning: Blood Findings: Microcytic hypochromic anemia Basophilic stippling of RBCs Cabot rings ↑ Zinc protoporphyrin (ZnPP) ↑ Free erythrocyte protoporphyrin (FEP) ↑ Blood lead levels (>5 µg/dL is significant; >40 µg/dL may show symptoms) Urine Findings: ↑ Urinary ALA (>5 µg/L) ↑ Urinary coproporphyrin (>150 µg/L) ↑ Urinary lead (>0.25 mg/L) Radiological Findings (especially in children): "Lead lines" (dense metaphyseal bands) seen at long bone metaphyses due to inhibited osteoclastic activity. Special Tests: Calcium disodium EDTA mobilization test (especially in children) to assess response to chelation therapy. Pathophysiology of Coproporphyrin Elevation: Lead inhibits the enzymes involved in the conversion of porphyrin precursors to heme, including: δ-ALA dehydratase Ferrochelatase This leads to an accumulation of porphyrin intermediates like coproporphyrin and ALA, which are excreted in urine and used diagnostically. Explanation of other options: Berylliosis (Option B): Occupational granulomatous lung disease due to beryllium exposure. Diagnosed via imaging and lung biopsy, not associated with porphyrin abnormalities. Silicosis (Option C): Caused by inhalation of silica dust leading to nodular pulmonary fibrosis. Diagnosis is based on chest imaging and history of exposure, not urinary porphyrin tests. Asbestosis (Option D): Chronic interstitial lung disease from asbestos exposure. Diagnosed via imaging (e.g., pleural plaques on X-ray/CT), not via heme biosynthesis markers.

expl: Hemoglobinopathies are autosomal codominant traits-thus, compound heterozygotes who inherit a different abnormal mutant allele from each parent exhibit composite features of each. For example, patients inheriting sickle β thalassemia exhibit features of β thalassemia and sickle cell anemia. text: What is the gene mutation associated with Marfan syndrome?
expl: Explanation: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder caused by mutations in the FBN1 gene on chromosome 15, which encodes fibrillin-1 , an important component of elastic fibres. Defective fibrillin leads to abnormal connective tissue, causing skeletal (tall stature, long limbs), ocular (lens subluxation), and cardiovascular manifestations (aortic root dilation, dissection) . Explanation of other options: FGFR3 (Option B): Mutation causes achondroplasia , leading to short-limb dwarfism, not Marfan's tall stature. COL1A1 (Option C): Mutations cause osteogenesis imperfecta , characterised by brittle bones, blue sclera, and hearing loss. TSC1 (Option D): Mutation causes tuberous sclerosis , a neurocutaneous syndrome with cortical tubers, seizures, and skin lesions.

expl: The answer is A (Increased amplitude of QRS complex): Athletic Heart Syndrome Athletic Heart Syndrome is a benign condition consisting of physiologic adaptations to the increased cardiac workload of exercise in trained athletes. text: A 70-year-old male presents with recurrent fainting episodes. His ECG shows P waves at a rate of 75 bpm and QRS complexes at a rate of 35 bpm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The clinical manifestations indicate Stokes Adams syndrome - sudden, transient episodes of syncope resulting from intermittent complete heart block or severe bradyarrhythmia. The ECG findings show P waves at 75 bpm with QRS complexes at 35 bpm , demonstrating AV dissociation typical of complete heart block or IIIrd degree heart block . This indicates a complete interruption of electrical conduction between the atria and ventricles, leading to independent atrial and ventricular rhythms. Third-degree atrioventricular block Refers to the complete failure of conduction between atria and ventricles, resulting in independent beating (AV dissociation). Ventricular Activity is maintained by an escape rhythm from: The AV node or bundle of His (narrow QRS complexes). Distal Purkinje tissues (broad QRS complexes). Clinical features Recurrent syncope or 'Stokes-Adams' attacks- sudden loss of consciousness and collapse. Brief anoxic seizure. Pallor and a death-like appearance during the attack; characteristic flush upon recovery. Rapid recovery distinguishes it from epilepsy. ECG Findings Prolonged PR interval Broad QRS complex Number of P waves will not be equal to the number of R waves P-R interval (atrial rate) will not match the R-R interval (ventricular rate) Fig: ECG showing complete heart block - AV dissociation, with the atrial rate (~100 bpm) independent of the ventricular rate (~40 bpm). Management Transient AV block in acute inferior myocardial infarction, requires no treatment if the patient remains stable. Symptomatic third-degree AV block are managed with intravenous atropine or intravenous isoprenaline to maintain circulation until temporary pacing is inserted. Permanent pacemaker. Explanation of other options: Mobitz type II heart block (Option A): A form of 2nd degree AV block in which there is intermittent non-conducted P waves without progressive prolongation of the PR interval. Thus, in Mobitz type II heart block there is normal PR intervals of 200ms. First degree heart block (Option C): A first degree heart block will show prolonged PR interval >200ms with 1:1 AV conduction. This is typically asymptomatic and would not cause the presenting symptoms of recurrent syncope. Wolf-Parkinson white syndrome (Option D): WPW Syndrome refers to the presence of a congenital accessory pathway (AP) and episodes of tachyarrhythmias. It presents with a short PR interval

text: A 30-year-old man is brought to ER with severe acute chest pain radiating to the back. He is pale and anxious.On examination the blood pressure is 150/90 mmHg and he was noted to have blue sclerae. Which of the following conditions has predisposed to this complication?
expl: Marfan's syndrome is one of the causes of blue sclerae. The clinical diagnosis is aortic dissection. Disorders predisposing to aortic dissection are: essential hypertension, atherosclerosis, bicuspid aortic valve, connective tissue disorders, Marfan's syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, adult polycystic kidney disease. Marfan's syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder caused by a defect in the fibrillin-1 gene on chromosome 15 . Clinical features: Tall stature with arm span to height ratio > 1.05 Upper to lower body ratio is decreased (head to symphysis pubis: symphysis pubis to toes). High-arched palate Arachnodactyly Pectus excavatum Pes planus Scoliosis of > 20 degrees à Low back pain Dural ectasia (ballooning of the dural sac at the lumbosacral level) – seen in 60% of patients. It may cause lower back pain associated with neurological problems such as bladder and bowel dysfunction like incontinence. Heart - Dilatation of the aortic sinuses (seen in 90%) which may lead to aortic regurgitation, aortic aneurysm, aortic dissection, and mitral valve prolapse (75%) which causes systolic murmur at mitral area. Lungs: repeated pneumothoraxes Eyes: Upwards lens dislocation (supertemporal ectopia lentis), blue sclera, retinal detachment and myopia. The life expectancy of patients used to be around 40-50 years. With the advent of regular echocardiography monitoring and beta-blocker/ACE inhibitor therapy this has improved significantly over recent years. Aortic dissection and other cardiovascular problems remain the leading cause of death however. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:274 pg:1917

text: A 40-year female has several episodes of vomiting and loose stool. She was managed at the periphery by IV fluids and hyponatremia was corrected. She presented to ER with paralysis, dysarthria, dysphagia, loss of consciousness. What might be the cause?

options.D: Excessive infusion fluids leading to fluid overload

expl: Overly rapid correction of hyponatremia (>8-10 mM in 24 h or 18 mM in 48 h) causes Osmotic demyelination syndrome. Hypertonic stress in astrocytes within brain regions prone to ODS, leading to generalized protein ubiquitination and endoplasmic reticulum stress due to activation of the unfolded protein response; this is accompanied by apoptotic and autophagic cell death. Rapid correction of hyponatremia also causes a disruption in integrity of the blood-brain barrier, allowing the entry of immune mediators that may contribute to demyelination. The lesions of ODS classically affect the pons, a neuroanatomic structure wherein the delay in the reaccumulation of osmotic osmolytes is particularly pronounced; clinically, patients with central pontine myelinolysis can present 1 or more days after overcorrection of hyponatremia with paraparesis or quadriparesis, dysphagia, dysarthria, diplopia, a "locked-in syndrome" , and/or loss of consciousness. Other regions of the brain can also be involved in ODS, most commonly in association with lesions of the pons but occasionally in isolation; in order of frequency, the lesions of extrapontine myelinolysis can occur in the cerebellum, lateral geniculate body, thalamus, putamen, and cerebral cortex or subcortex. Clinical presentation of ODS can, therefore, vary as a function of the extent and localization of extrapontine myelinolysis, with the reported development of ataxia, mutism, parkinsonism, dystonia, and catatonia. However, even appropriately slow correction can be associated with ODS, particularly in patients with additional risk factors; these include alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalemia, and liver transplantation.

text: A patient presents with spastic quadriplegia. What is the most likely site of lesion?
expl: Explanation: Periventricular leukomalacia (PVL) refers to ischemic necrosis of the white matter adjacent to the lateral ventricles, typically seen in preterm infants due to hypoxic-ischemic injury . It affects the descending corticospinal tracts → spasticity and motor deficits . If extensive, both upper and lower limbs are affected → spastic quadriplegia . Pathogenesis: Hypoxia → ischemia of watershed zones near ventricles → demyelination and necrosis → cystic cavitations in periventricular white matter. Explanation of Other Options: Basal ganglia calcification (Option B): Seen in hypoparathyroidism or Fahr's disease . Produces extrapyramidal symptoms (rigidity, tremor, dystonia). Does not cause spasticity or pyramidal signs. Usually bilateral and symmetric on CT scan. Cerebellar degeneration (Option C): Causes ataxia , dysmetria, intention tremor, and hypotonia. Gait becomes wide-based and unsteady . No hyperreflexia or spastic quadriplegia. Seen in chronic alcoholism , paraneoplastic syndromes , or vitamin E deficiency . Cystic encephalomalacia (Option D): Post-hypoxic destruction of brain parenchyma forming cystic cavities . Causes focal neurological deficits depending on area affected. Usually results in seizures or cognitive delay , not pure spasticity. Common sequel of severe hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.

text: A 49-year-old man presents with flu-like symptoms and a palmoplantar rash. On examination, epitrochlear lymphadenopathy is noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The classic rash and accompanying symptoms strongly suggest a diagnosis of secondary syphilis. Key Features of Secondary Syphilis: Mucocutaneous and cutaneous lesions along with generalized, non-tender lymphadenopathy. The primary chancre may still be present in about 15% of cases, particularly more common in HIV-positive individuals. Skin Rash: Presents as macular, papular, papulosquamous, or sometimes pustular lesions (syphilides). Lesions can be subtle, and up to 25% of patients with visible rash may not notice it. Typically begin as pale red or pink, non-itchy macules on the trunk and limbs. Progress to papular lesions, often involving the palms and soles. In HIV patients, severe necrotic lesions known as lues maligna can occur. Hair and Mucosal Involvement: Patchy hair loss on the scalp, eyebrows, or beard occurs in about 5% of cases. Condylomata lata- moist, highly infectious lesions can develop in skin folds such as the perianal area, vulva, or scrotum (seen in 10% of cases). Mucous patches, painless silver-gray erosions, commonly appear on oral or genital mucosa in 10-15% of patients. Constitutional Symptoms: Sore throat (15-30%), fever (5-8%), weight loss (2-20%), malaise (25%), anorexia (2-10%), headache (10%), and meningismus (5%). Acute meningitis may occur in 1-2% of patients, with cerebrospinal fluid abnormalities seen in up to 40% of early syphilis cases. Ocular and Ear Involvement: Ocular symptoms include pupillary changes, optic neuritis, iritis, or uveitis, which can cause permanent vision loss if untreated. Ear symptoms may include sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo, or tinnitus. Less Common Complications: Hepatitis, kidney disease, gastrointestinal conditions (such as hypertrophic gastritis and proctitis), arthritis, and periostitis. Liver involvement is often asymptomatic, while renal issues arise from immune complex deposition, leading to proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome. Resolution: Most signs and symptoms of secondary syphilis resolve spontaneously within 1 to 6 months. Options A, C and D are incorrect.

text: Elective splenectomy is preferred in which of the given conditions?
expl: Explanation: Hereditary spherocytosis is a genetic condition where red blood cells are sphere-shaped rather than biconcave, and the main treatment is elective splenectomy. In hereditary spherocytosis , splenectomy is highly beneficial since the spleen is chiefly responsible for destroying spherocytes. The timing depends on disease severity: In severe cases it is done electively at 4-6 years, in moderate cases, it may be postponed until adolescence , while mild cases are usually managed with folic acid supplementation alone. Explanations of other options: G6PD deficiency (Option A): In G6PD deficiency, splenectomy can aggravate anaemia since the spleen plays a key role in clearing damaged red blood cells. Management mainly focuses on preventing exposure to oxidative triggers and treating acute hemolytic crises. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (Option B): In paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), hemolysis results from a complement system defect, making stem cell transplantation the only curative option. Splenectomy is not useful since the red cell destruction is complement-driven and occurs in the entire circulation. Hairy cell leukaemia (Option D): In hairy cell leukaemia, the primary treatment is chemotherapy , while splenectomy is reserved for patients with significant splenomegaly or those who do not respond to standard therapy, rather than being the first-line approach.

text: Which microorganism causes cat scratch disease?
expl: Explanation: Cat scratch disease (CSD) is an infection caused by Bartonella henselae , a Gram-negative, facultative intracellular bacterium. It is transmitted by the bite or scratch of cats (especially kittens) or via fleas carrying infected feces. In immunocompetent patients, it causes localized lymphadenopathy and fever, while in immunocompromised individuals, it can lead to bacillary angiomatosis, peliosis hepatis, and endocarditis. Transmission: Primarily from cats; via scratches, bites, or fleas (Ctenocephalides felis). Clinical presentations: Cat scratch disease (immunocompetent): Papule/pustule at site, tender lymphadenopathy, fever, malaise. Bacillary angiomatosis (immunocompromised): Vascular skin lesions resembling Kaposi sarcoma, systemic symptoms. Peliosis hepatis: Blood-filled cavities in liver/spleen, hepatomegaly. Endocarditis: Culture-negative, seen in immunocompromised patients. Diagnosis: Serology (IgM/IgG via ELISA/IFA), PCR, Warthin-Starry silver stain, culture (difficult). Treatment: CSD: Often self-limiting. Severe → azithromycin or doxycycline. Bacillary angiomatosis/peliosis: Doxycycline or erythromycin for months. Endocarditis: Doxycycline + rifampin. Explanation of other options: B. quintana (Option B): Causes trench fever, spread by lice. B. bacilliformis (Option C): Causes Carrion's disease, transmitted by sandflies. Borrelia burgdorferi (Option D): Causes Lyme disease via tick bites. Key Takeaways: Bartonella henselae is the causative agent of cat scratch disease. In immunocompromised hosts, the infection manifests as bacillary angiomatosis or peliosis hepatis .

text: A 27-year-old shop worker is referred with a three month history of recurrent episodes of disorientation and confusion. Her friend has found her wandering around the house on several occasions, apparently with no idea of where she is or how she got there. Her mood has been very low, with frequent emotional outbursts, and she has considered leaving her job because of problems with working the computer and managing customers' queries. Her friend feels her condition is significantly worsening. Physical examination is normal, apart from recurrent, asymetrical, jerks in all four limbs. Which of the following investigations is likely to be most useful in reaching a diagnosis?
expl: This kind of rapid cognitive decline in a young person with myoclonus is strongly suggestive of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD). A definitive diagnosis of any form of CJD requires pathological examination of brain tissue, which is usually only done post-mortem. During life, investigations are undertaken for two reasons: to exclude other possible diagnoses, and to support the diagnosis of CJD. Supportive investigations are EEG, CSF examination and MRI. The EEG in sporadic CJD may show significant abnormalities involving deep brain areas such as the thalami. The normal rhythms are gradually lost. Initially the changes are diffuse, and non-specific, developing into generalised bi- or triphasic periodic sharp wave complexes with a frequency of 1-2 per second. High voltage sharp waves may be synchronous with myoclonic jerks. In an appropriate clinical context, this EEG pattern is strongly suggestive of a diagnosis of CJD. Neither CSF examination nor MRI are options here, but both can also give supportive information. The CSF typically contains no inflammatory cells, but the total protein content may be raised. Analysis for brain specific proteins, particularly 14-3-3, is supportive in the right clinical context. In a proportion of cases, abnormalities of signal in the anterior basal ganglia (caudate/putamen, and sometimes the cortex) can be seen on MRI, which can also support the diagnosis. Chest x ray and liver function tests may help to exclude other diagnoses, but do not give supportive information for CJD. Visual evoked potentials may be altered in CJD, but no specific pattern has yet been identified to support the diagnosis. CT head generally demonstrates brain atrophy in CJD, but this is not a specific finding and is therefore less useful than an EEG. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 438, Pg: 3420 20th edition Chapter:430 Page number:3152-3153
